summary: This experimental memo describes how to translate between X.400 message handling systems and Mail-11, also called DECnet mail, so the two kinds of mail systems can exchange messages. It was replaced by RFC 2162.

eli5.summary: Two mail systems that speak different languages need a translator. This paper explains how to turn messages from one kind of email into the other so they can understand each other.

questions: how does x400 address translate to mail-11
subtitle: How to translate messages between two different email systems

tldr.problem: X.400 and Mail-11 (DECnet mail) are two different email systems with different message formats and addressing schemes. Users on networks using one system cannot easily exchange mail with users on networks using the other.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines mapping rules to convert messages and addresses between X.400 and Mail-11, including how to translate message elements and convert addresses from one format to the other, with support for routing through multiple gateways.
tldr.outcome: This RFC enabled hybrid networks to use gateways that bridge X.400 and Mail-11 systems, allowing users in each system to communicate. It was replaced by RFC 2162 with updates to the mapping scheme.

today: RFC 1405 is an experimental protocol that was replaced by RFC 2162, which provides updated mapping rules. Mail-11 and DECnet Phase IV networks are now largely historical, having been replaced by modern IP-based systems. However, the principles of gateway-based protocol translation and the technique of using Domain Defined Attributes to preserve original addressing information remain relevant for understanding multi-protocol network gateways.

sections.title: The Two Email Systems
sections.content:
This RFC describes mappings between two different email protocols: X.400 and Mail-11.

X.400 is the CCITT X.400 Series Recommendations for Message-Oriented Text Interchange Service (MOTIS), covering Inter-Personal Messaging System (IPMS). X.400 is a complex, standards-based system with many sophisticated features.

Mail-11, also known as DECnet mail, is Digital Equipment Corporation's proprietary protocol for real-time text messaging over DECnet Phase IV networks. It is simpler than X.400.

Large communities using Mail-11 include the High Energy Physics network (HEPnet) and the Space Physics Analysis Network (SPAN). These DECnet communities may eventually migrate to DECnet Phase V (DECnet-OSI) and merge into X.400, but the transition period will be long and some DECnet Phase IV communities may persist. Therefore, mapping rules between Mail-11 and X.400 are necessary.

The RFC also considers RFC 822, the standard for personal messaging in the Internet, which sits between the two systems. The complete scenario of X.400, RFC 822, and Mail-11 is covered to handle complex gateway translations.
sections.eli5: X.400 is a fancy email system used in many places. Mail-11 is a simpler system used on DECnet networks. People using each system need to be able to send mail to the other, so we need translation rules.

sections.title: Message and Service Element Mapping
sections.content:
Mail-11 protocol offers a restricted set of elements composing an Inter-Personal Message (IPM), while X.400 supports a complex and large amount of service elements. When a message is relayed between two X.400 systems via a DECnet network, the simpler Mail-11 format would cause nearly complete loss of information.

To minimize this problem, most X.400 service elements are mapped into Mail-11 text body parts. Mail-11 envelope (P1) and header (P2) elements map directly: P1.From maps to P1.Originator, P1.To maps to P1.Primary Recipient, P2.From maps to P2.Originator, P2.To maps to P2.Primary Recipient, Cc maps to Copy Recipient, Date maps to Submission Time Stamp, and Subject maps to Subject.

X.400 service elements map in the reverse direction to Mail-11. Primary Recipients map to 'To', Copy Recipients map to 'Cc', and Submission Time Stamp maps to 'date'. The Blind Copy Recipient element receives special handling: a new message is created with a separate envelope for the BCC recipient, preserving privacy, and notes are added informing all recipients about the BCC action.

Any other X.400 service element is handled according to RFC 1327, with the mapped element included in an RFC 822-like header within the Mail-11 body part. This approach preserves as much information as possible when translating between the systems.
sections.eli5: Mail-11 messages are simpler than X.400 messages. To translate them, we take the basic information (from, to, subject) and translate it directly. For fancy features Mail-11 does not support, we turn them into text that goes in the message body.

sections.title: Address Format and Translation
sections.content:
Mail-11 addresses are ASCII strings with three optional parts: route (a path through DECnet nodes), node (the destination DECnet node), and local-part (the user). Only the local-part is compulsory. The local-part can be a username, nickname, or a foreign-protocol reference containing an address for another system (RFC 822, X.400, or other).

Examples of Mail-11 addresses include simple names like USER47, node-addressed names like MYNODE::BETTY, routed names like BOSTON::CLUS02::GOOFY1::MARY34, and foreign-protocol references like IN%"M.P.Tracy@Dicdum.cc.edu".

X.400 O/R (Originator/Recipient) addresses are collections of attributes that can be represented as IA5 textual form. The basic mapping rule converts a Mail-11 address route::node::localpart into an X.400 address with country code, ADMD, PRMD, organization, organizational unit, and two Domain Defined Attributes: DD.Dnet (the DECnet network name) and DD.Mail-11 (the original Mail-11 address).

To uniquely identify each DECnet network, a network name (such as HEPnet, SPAN, or Enet) is introduced. This allows intelligent gateways to route messages correctly even when multiple isolated Mail-11 networks use the same address space. A registry of network names and their corresponding gateway addresses must be maintained to ensure uniqueness.
sections.eli5: Mail-11 addresses are like postcards with a name and maybe some routing information. X.400 addresses are like formal letters with many fields. We translate by putting the Mail-11 address into specific X.400 fields and remember which DECnet network it came from.

sections.title: The Mapping Process
sections.content:
The RFC defines mapping rules in both directions: Mail-11 to X.400 and X.400 to Mail-11.

When mapping Mail-11 to X.400, the gateway creates an X.400 address using the country code, ADMD, and PRMD of the gateway performing the conversion, plus the organization and organizational unit that identify the gateway uniquely. The DECnet network name is stored in DD.Dnet, and the original Mail-11 address is preserved in DD.Mail-11. If the node is missing from the Mail-11 address, defaults apply: for originators, it defaults to the DECnet node name of the gateway; for recipients, it defaults to the node of the originator.

When mapping X.400 to Mail-11, path reversibility is important for multi-hop translations. If the DD.Dnet value is known to the gateway as one of its connected DECnet networks, the mapping is trivial: the DD.Mail-11 value is extracted directly. If DD.Dnet is not known to the gateway, the gateway encodes the entire X.400 address into the Mail-11 local-part as a foreign-protocol reference, preserving all information so the next gateway can decode it.

The RFC also covers the complex scenario where a message originates from an RFC 822 system, is relayed through Mail-11, and arrives at X.400. The mappings specified in RFC 1327 and its updates are used to produce an RFC 822-like header, ensuring consistent translation across all three systems.
sections.eli5: When translating Mail-11 to X.400, we fill in the X.400 form fields with the right information and remember the original Mail-11 address. When translating back, we try to recreate the original format. If we can not, we encode the X.400 address as text inside the Mail-11 message so the next computer can decode it.

sections.title: Gateways and Network Naming
sections.content:
A key innovation is the concept of the DECnet network name (net), a unique ASCII string identifying a DECnet community. Examples include HEPnet (High Energy Physics), SPAN (Space Physics Analysis Network), and Enet (Digital's corporate network).

Because multiple isolated DECnet networks can use the same address space, gateways must be able to distinguish which network a message originated from. A registry mapping network names to gateway addresses enables this. The registry is implemented as a simple table in a syntax similar to RFC 1327's gate table. Ambiguous entries with multiple gateways for a network are allowed; gateway implementations can choose one or try all in cyclic order for better performance.

An intelligent gateway understands its own connectivity and can route messages appropriately even when the X.400 address specifies a path to a different gateway. This flexibility is crucial for hybrid networks spanning multiple DECnet communities.

The RFC defines the notation and examples for Mail-11 addresses with various complexities, from simple local users to routed addresses crossing multiple DECnet nodes, to addresses containing foreign-protocol references (X.400, RFC 822, UUCP, etc.). The mapping scheme handles all these cases using Domain Defined Attributes and the foreign-protocol reference notation.
sections.eli5: Gateways are like post offices that translate between two mail systems. They keep a list of DECnet networks they know about and which other gateways serve them. Smart gateways can figure out the best route even if the address suggests a different one.
